plain_english: First on my list are people who spend their time drinking and indulging themselves. No one wastes time more shamefully than they do. At least other people — even the greedy, the angry, those who hate for no reason or start pointless wars — are chasing something that looks like glory. You can criticize them, but they're still pursuing something that seems important to them. They sin, but they sin like human beings. But people who live only for food and pleasure? That's just disgraceful. Look at how these gluttons and pleasure-seekers spend their hours. How much time do they spend scheming? How much worrying? How much giving fake compliments or receiving them? How much time signing contracts and making deals? How much at dinner parties that become serious business themselves? You'll see they get no rest from either their pleasures or their troubles.
original_excerpt: Among these I reckon in the first place those who devote their time to nothing but drinking and debauchery: for no men are busied more shamefully: the others, although the glory which they pursue is but a counterfeit, still deserve some credit for their pursuit of it—though you may tell me of misers, of passionate men, of men who hate and who even wage war without a cause—yet all such men sin like men: but the sin of those who are given up to gluttony and lust is a disgraceful one. Examine all the hours of their lives: consider how much time they spend in calculation, how much in plotting, how much in fear, how much in giving and deceiving flattery, how much in entering into recognizances for themselves or for others, how much in banquets, which indeed become a serious business, you will see that they are not allowed any breathing time either by their pleasures or their pains.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: Everyone agrees on this: you can't do anything well — whether speaking or writing — if your mind is busy with other things. Nothing takes deep root in a mind that's constantly distracted and pushes away whatever you try to put into it. No one knows less about living than a businessman. There's nothing harder to learn than how to live. You can find teachers for other skills everywhere. Some skills are so simple that children can master them and then teach others. But learning how to live takes your entire lifetime. And what might surprise you even more — learning how to die also takes your entire lifetime.
original_excerpt: Finally, all are agreed that nothing, neither eloquence nor literature, can be done properly by one who is occupied with something else; for nothing can take deep root in a mind which is directed to some other subject, and which rejects whatever you try to stuff into it. No man knows less about living than a business man: there is nothing about which it is more difficult to gain knowledge. Other arts have many folk everywhere who profess to teach them: some of them can be so thoroughly learned by mere boys, that they are able to teach them to others: but one's whole life must be spent in learning how to live, and, which may perhaps surprise you more, one's whole life must be spent in learning how to die.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english:
Many excellent people have freed themselves from all distractions. They've given up wealth, business deals, and pleasures. They've made it their life's work to learn how to live well. Yet most of them die admitting they still don't know how to live — let alone how to live wisely.

Believe me, it takes a great person to protect their time from being stolen. Someone who rises above human weaknesses won't let anyone take even a minute from them. That's why their life feels very long — they give every possible moment to themselves. No part of their time sits idle or wasted or under someone else's control. They find nothing worth trading their time for, and they guard it fiercely.

Such a person has enough time. But those who give most of their lives to other people will always run short.
original_excerpt: Many excellent men have freed themselves from all hindrances, have given up riches, business, and pleasure, and have made it their duty to the very end of their lives to learn how to live: and yet the larger portion of them leave this life confessing that they do not yet know how to live, and still less know how to live as wise men. Believe me, it requires a great man and one who is superior to human frailties not to allow any of his time to be filched from him: and therefore it follows that his life is a very long one, because he devotes every possible part of it to himself: no portion lies idle or uncultivated, or in another man's power; for he finds nothing worthy of being exchanged for his time, which he husbands most grudgingly. He, therefore, had time enough: whereas those who gave up a great part of their lives to the people of necessity had not enough.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: But don't think wealthy people are unaware of what they're losing. You'll often hear those blessed with great success cry out, even surrounded by their crowds of followers and important legal cases: "I can't live my own life!" Why can't he? Because everyone who calls on him for help steals him away from himself. How many days have you lost to that client you're defending? To that person running for office? To that old woman tired of outliving her heirs? To that man faking illness to make his potential inheritors more eager? To that powerful friend who uses you as decoration in his entourage, not as a real friend? Add it all up. Go through every day of your life. You'll find that only a handful of days — the ones too worthless for anyone else to claim — were actually yours.
original_excerpt: Yet you need not suppose that the latter were not sometimes conscious of their loss: indeed, you will hear most of those who are troubled with great prosperity every now and then cry out amid their hosts of clients, their pleadings in court, and their other honourable troubles, "I am not allowed to live my own life." Why is he not allowed? because all those who call upon you to defend them, take you away from yourself. How many of your days have been spent by that defendant? by that candidate for office? by that old woman who is weary with burying her heirs? by that man who pretends to be ill, in order to excite the greed of those who hope to inherit his property? by that powerful friend of yours, who uses you to swell his train, not to be his friend? Balance your account, and run over all the days of your life; you will see that only a very few days, and only those which were useless for any other purpose, have been left to you.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: The person who gets the political office he desperately wanted now can't wait to get rid of it. He keeps saying, "When will this year be over?" Another person puts on expensive public games — something he once would have paid dearly for the chance to do. Now he asks, "When can I escape from this?" Another is a famous lawyer who packs the courtrooms. Crowds fill the entire forum, stretching far beyond where they can even hear him speak. But he asks, "When will vacation time come?" Everyone rushes through life. They long for the future and feel tired of the present. But the person who uses all his time for his own purposes — who plans each day as if he's planning his whole life — doesn't wish for tomorrow or fear it. What new pleasure could any hour bring him? He knows it all. He's experienced it all, even to the point of being sick of it.
original_excerpt: He who has obtained the _fasces_[6] for which he longed, is eager to get rid of them, and is constantly saying, "When will this year be over?" another exhibits public games, and once would have given a great deal for the chance of doing so, but now "when," says he, "shall I escape from this?" another is an advocate who is fought for in all the courts, and who draws immense audiences, who crowd all the forum to a far greater distance than they can hear him; "When," says he, "will vacation-time come?" Every man hurries through his life, and suffers from a yearning for the future, and a weariness of the present: but he who disposes of all his time for his own purposes, who arranges all his days as though he were arranging the plan of his life, neither wishes for nor fears the morrow: for what new pleasure can any hour now bestow upon him? he knows it all, and has indulged in it all even to satiety.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: Fortune can do what she wants with everything else — this man's life is already protected from her. He might gain something, but he can't lose anything. He can only gain things the way someone who's already stuffed with food might take another bite even though he doesn't want it. So don't assume someone has lived a long life just because he has wrinkles or gray hair. That person hasn't lived long — he's just been alive for a long time. Think about it this way: would you say a sailor had traveled far if a storm caught him right after leaving port and kept spinning him in circles with winds blowing from every direction? That sailor didn't travel much. He just got tossed around a lot.
original_excerpt: Fortune may deal with the rest as she will, his life is already safe from her: such a man may gain something, but cannot lose anything: and, indeed, he can only gain anything in the same way as one who is already glutted and filled can get some extra food which he takes although he does not want it. You have no grounds, therefore, for supposing that any one has lived long, because he has wrinkles or grey hairs: such a man has not lived long, but has only been long alive. Why! would you think that a man had voyaged much if a fierce gale had caught him as soon as he left his port, and he had been driven round and round the same place continually by a succession of winds blowing from opposite quarters? such a man has not travelled much, he has only been much tossed about.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7
